tagline: Auto-generate burned-in captions for short videos and crop them to vertical with basic face tracking.
verdictSummary: Transcribing a video locally with Whisper, burning styled captions onto it with ffmpeg, and cropping to a vertical 9:16 frame using basic face detection to keep the speaker centered is a genuine consolation build — a real one-sitting project that produces a usable captioned clip. It approximates Captions' reframe with a much simpler face-tracking heuristic, not the trained model that keeps a shot framed through fast motion and multiple speakers.
coreLoopDIY: Transcribe a local video with Whisper, generate word-level caption timing, burn styled captions into the frame with ffmpeg, and crop to a vertical frame using face detection to keep whoever's speaking roughly centered.
whatYouLose: a trained reframe model that tracks speakers reliably through fast cuts and multiple people in frame
a phone-native mobile app for recording and captioning on the go
a licensed catalog of AI avatar presenters
cloud rendering, so exports don't queue behind your own machine
caption style presets tuned and tested across thousands of videos
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for Captions because a simple face-detection heuristic loses track of the subject the moment there's fast motion, a hand gesture blocking the face, or more than one person talking — Captions' model was trained specifically to keep tracking through exactly those cases. The subscription buys that reliability under real recording conditions, not just captions and a crop.
prompt:
Build a local video-captioning tool: transcribe, burn in styled captions, and crop to vertical with basic face tracking. Stack: Python, ffmpeg for all video processing, whisper.cpp for local transcription, OpenCV for face detection. No cloud API required.

Core loop: the user drops in a local video file. Transcribe it with whisper.cpp to get word-level timestamps, then generate an ASS subtitle track with styled, word-by-word highlighted captions and burn it into the video with ffmpeg. Separately, run OpenCV's face detector on sampled frames, smooth the detected face position across time, and compute a vertical 9:16 crop window that follows it — falling back to a fixed center crop for stretches with no detected face. Export the final captioned, cropped video as a single file.

This needs no API key — whisper.cpp and OpenCV both run fully offline. A GPU speeds up transcription but isn't required for typical short-clip lengths.

Do not build: a trained face/subject-tracking model (this uses off-the-shelf OpenCV detection, explicitly weaker under fast motion or multiple speakers — say so in the UI when confidence is low), AI avatar presenters, or a mobile app. If OpenCV loses the face for more than a couple of seconds, fall back to center crop rather than guessing.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Captions projects?
faq.a: No — Captions' project files and caption styles are internal to their app. You'd start from your raw video files and reapply your preferred caption look once as a reusable template.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: No — ffmpeg processing and face detection need more compute than a typical phone browser provides. You'd record on your phone, then run this on a computer to process.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing per video — whisper.cpp and OpenCV both run locally with no per-minute charge. The only cost is the compute time itself, which is free if it's your own machine.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Reliable tracking through motion. Captions' model keeps the crop centered on a moving, gesturing speaker or switches correctly between multiple people talking; the OpenCV-based heuristic here loses the face regularly under exactly those conditions and just holds a static crop until it reacquires it.
